item.title: Protecting Children From the Effects of Parental Burnout
item.description:
Burnout

Protecting Children From the Effects of Parental Burnout

Understanding the link between parental stress and caring for children.

Posted October 4, 2026

Key points
  • Parental burnout is commonly experienced by new mothers and fathers.
  • A risk factor for burnout-related behavior is feeling overwhelmed and undersupported.
  • Recognizing red flags of negative emotion helps new parents seek help sooner.

Becoming a parent is one of the most precious, rewarding experiences in life. It can also be both exhilarating and terrifying for new parents who feel overwhelmed and undersupported. Many are juggling childcare with jobs, other family responsibilities, errands, and making ends meet. In some cases, due to their circumstances, parents may be uniquely susceptible to negative parenting practices leading to dysfunctional relationships with children. Research explains.

Source: Alena Konstantin/Pixabay

Baby Burnout Blues

Katherine M. Ryan et al. (2026) explored the impact of parental burnout within families who are at risk of child neglect or abuse.[i] They define parental burnout as including feelings of exhaustion, emotional distancing from children, and experiencing a decline in the capacity to effectively parent. Ryan et al. distinguish parental burnout from the stress of daily parenting and parent mental health by its association with the perception of overwhelming demands paired with insufficient coping resources.

Far from being unusual, Ryan et al. note that parental burnout is actually quite common among parents who are raising young children. Within community samples, they note that parents of young children report high levels of emotional exhaustion, and according to the Office of the Surgeon General (2024), about one-third of parents of young children experience extremely high levels of burnout.

These statistics are uniquely important to consider within families who, due to other circumstances, may be at risk of aggression or unhealthy patterns of behavior.

Households At Risk

Ryan et al. used a sample of study participants who were 140 Australian caregivers who had been referred to a parenting support program as a result of substantiated child abuse or neglect, or a combination of family stress and having a child who presented significant externalizing behaviors. Participants shared a variety of experienced emotional symptoms, as well as parenting behaviors, both positive, such as involvement and warmth, and negative, such as hostility and coercion.

Ryan et al. found that, as reported, total burnout was specifically linked with decreased positive and increased negative parenting behaviors. They also found a unique link between parental mental health and less positive parenting, and child externalizing behavior and more negative parenting. They concluded, among other things, that parental burnout is uniquely associated with reduced parental warmth and support, as well as a higher level of hostility and coercion towards children within families who are at risk.

Regarding how the negative cycle works, Ryan et al. note that some families are uniquely susceptible to coercive parent-child interaction due to extra demands and coping challenges. They explain that hostile, ineffective, or withdrawn parenting behaviors as well as distressing emotional responses reinforce children's externalizing behaviors, which can fuel tantrums, angry outbursts, and aggressive behavior. They further note that parental burnout may lead to more hostile or coercive strategies when children are engaging in disruptive behaviors, and conversely, children's disruptive externalizing behaviors could fuel parental burnout.

Breaking Burnout: The Parental Road to Recovery

Some parents who admit feeling overwhelmed are relieved to find they are in good company. Not only are feelings of burnout more common than many people realize, but there is also a wide variety of methods to help tone down negative feelings and treat emotional exhaustion. Family, friends, neighbors, and faith-based institutions are all potential sources of support to help new parents maintain their sense of balance.

One goal when working with parents experiencing burnout, especially if they are at risk or have already experienced negative cycles of behavior, is helping them recognize the red flags early. Noticing signs of irritability, self-blame, perceived incompetence, or a sense of hopelessness can remind parents to reach out for support, whether physical assistance with childcare while they take a break to rest and recharge, or psychological support to help them talk through stress, anxiety, or other negative emotions.

Working with a supportive network, new parents can improve their emotions, routines, and methods of interacting with their precious little ones to promote a healthy, happy future. And of course, for additional mental or emotional support, professional help is available.

item.title: Neuroscience Essentials: Chudler's "Neuropedia" Reviewed
item.description:
Neuroscience

Neuroscience Essentials: Chudler's "Neuropedia" Reviewed

A new book on all things brain reminds readers of the value of analog knowledge.

Posted October 4, 2026

Key points
  • "Neuropedia" offers a concise, analog guide to brain basics, illustrated for visual learning.
  • The brain’s redundancy enables some people to live without a corpus callosum, often without symptoms.
  • Split-brain cases raise deep questions about consciousness and personal identity.
Source: Princeton University Press

We're intimate with our brains. We could almost touch them, except for the skull and dura that protect them. We sense them at work, helping us think, feel, move, digest, breathe. But how exactly they're doing any of this is mysterious to most of us. Some of us may see fMRI or PET images of our brains, but those are pictures, not fats and proneins, not glial cells or neurons.

Enter neuroscientist Eric H. Chudler's Neuropedia, a mini-encyclopedia on all things brain. In 150 pages, illustrated by Kelly Chudler, this small book elucidates brain structures, functions, and conditions—along with entries on neuroscience luminaries—in clear, accessible prose. As Chudler writes, "I have tried to include entries that will stimulate your curiosity, help you become familiar with neurosciene, and motivate you to learn more about the brain." The aim is to introduce lay readers to crucial concepts with both accuracy and a healthy dash of fun.

Of course, it's no comprehensive account. As Chudler writes, "My intention is to open a window to the process of discovery that occurs in research laboratories every day."

The book's illustrations range from the instructive to the fanciful, inviting readers to combine curiosity and the wonder we may feel when contemplating those elusive three pounds of flesh that do so much to animate us—and to enable us to live and function in the world.

Explaining the Corpus Callosum and Redundancy in the Brain

Chuder, Neuropedia, p. 45
Source: Princeton Unviersity Press

For example, Chudler describes the corpus callosum as a "large collection of axons that connect the left and right hemispheres of the brain." It contains about 200 million axons "crossing from side to side to help coordinate sensory processes and higher cognitive functions of the brain." Observations about anatomy like this one can quickly turn philosophical. About 1 in 4,000 people are born without a corpus callosum, some of them experiencing no symptoms at all while others experience difficulties with vision, language, or motor coordination. This leads to an explanation of redundancy in the brain. If a person whose brain lacks what Chudler calls this "neural superhighway"—without symptoms—there must be other, generally redundant pathways performing similar functions.

This is the case with many brain structures, and the reason people with brain damage are able to restore lost functions. Other areas and structures adapt to perform the functions of damaged ones. The philosophical question arises: What is the relationship between physiology and experience? Neuroscience is beginning to hazard some answers, and they inevitably lead to yet more philosophical questions.

That's where a site like the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy comes in handy. In an entry on Split Brains, it explains that corpus collostomies—generally conducted to treat symptoms of severe seiziure disorders—can result in a splitting of consciousness without the patient realizing it. For example, "imagine presenting the word “TAXABLE” on a screen in front of a split-brain patient" so that "TAX" appears only to the left visual field and “ABLE” only to the right. "When asked to verbalize what word is being shown, the verbal response, typically controlled by the left hemisphere, will be 'ABLE.' However, if the patient is instructed to write down what they see using their left hand, which is predominantly controlled by the right hemisphere, they typically write 'TAX.'” What, then, are the implications for the identity of a person whose consciousness is split in this way?

Chudler, Neuropedia, p. 32
Source: Princeton Niversity Press

Comparing Neuropedia and Online Educational Resources

Neuropedia will provide the basics, and curious readers may follow up on questions both neurological and philosophical, using a site like Stanford's or Neuropedia.net, which describes itself as "an open-access, educational platform designed to provide scientific content through a structured curriculum." Sites like this can be overwhelming, with their wealth of information on disparate topics. The analog nature of Chudler's book makes for a very different kind of experience. The information it provides is contained, quite literally, between its covers. It may spark curiosity and offer brief explanations. If a reader wants to learn more, it can help focus an internet search. Nonetheless, the book's lively prose and elegant illustrations make for an analog experience all its own, an antidote to the overwhelm of endless clicks through the vast and often unreliable internet. This is a book that invites readers to focus and reflect rather than click and scroll.

With rapid advances in neuroscience reported in the news and finding their way into an array of movies and TV shows, we're increasingly surrounded by the language of neuroscience. But what does it all mean? Chudler's spare compendium is a useful guide to that language—and will almost certainly be more accurate and lead to greater understanding than most pop culture representations of the brain.

item.title: When the Need for Change Becomes a Trap
item.description:
Attachment

When the Need for Change Becomes a Trap

Are you moving forward or just moving?

Posted October 4, 2026

Key points
  • Seeking change can be an avoidant strategy.
  • Routine and stability can guard against encounter.
  • Healthy change is intrinsically motivated.

We often think of change as a good thing. Indeed, change is what we fundamentally work on or work toward in therapy. We ask: what are your goals or how would you like to change? Isn’t this exactly what we mean by growth?

The idea of change, however, can sometimes be linked to (or be a product of) its opposite—stasis, immobility, or even stuckness.

Someone who is constantly “on the move”—literally or psychologically—may be privately treading water.

Traveling and exploring, developing new social and friendship groups, or trying out new self-improvement strategies may all give the appearance of growth and change, but may conceal larger patterns of avoidance and fear.

How can this be so? A defence against attachment?

One way to look at frequent change may be through the lens of defences: is our need for change and movement a defence against stillness or boredom? Boredom is frequently seen as a problem to solve, and our culture participates in this by providing endless entertainments. There are many other potential feelings that lurk under boredom, however, and some may be worth exploring.

A restlessness may indicate a degree of dissatisfaction with the status quo—career, relationships or attachments in general. Some of us may struggle with a feeling of, “Is this it?” Or, “Is this all?”

Novelty and change offer a seeming solution to this crisis of stasis. But constant distractions can have an addictive quality, and boredom and addiction are frequently close bedfellows. Some of us would be wise to “catch up with ourselves” rather than forge ahead into new territory—to reflect and take stock of what we have achieved, failed to achieved, what we have loved, and what we have lost. Psychologically, this can mean learning to be alone with ourselves.

Stability as a Defence Against Encounter

Should we envy and model ourselves after those with a rigid and fixed routine, who never change, who practice self-restraint and temperance? Perhaps, but in some cases, the overly “stable” may be guarding against uncertainty and encounter, and likely restricting natural growth in the process.

In some ways, this can be very successful—to have found a formula for life that works. (If it ain’t broke, as they say...) The problem, however, is that life is inherently dynamic and dialectical—things change and break apart. New models and ways of being are very often needed throughout the lifespan and aging process. (We all know what sticking to a teenage diet will cost us long term…)

The restless person in search of change and the routine person who is risk averse may both reflect a pattern of repetition that shields them from real psychological change or movement. Both may be organized around avoiding uncertainty, disappointment, vulnerability, and the limits of their own choices.

A Healthy Relation to Change?

What would a healthy relation to change look like? In psychotherapy, we often track and look for organic and internal impulses for change. For instance, someone may be having a recurring dream motif or seemingly same relational patterns. When these are noticed and processed, they may produce frustration and an internal motivation to adjust life momentum. Change in these cases means changing patterns or repetitions that no longer serve us, whether those patterns are rooted in actual novelty-seeking or in routine.

Change and exploration can be incredible life moves. Routine and stability are also essential for a sense of security. The challenge is to discern when the motivation is intrinsic and self-initiating, and when it is a distraction or an avoidance to those same internal processes.

item.title: During Courtroom Drama, Consider the Courtroom Trauma
item.description:
Trauma

During Courtroom Drama, Consider the Courtroom Trauma

There is significant psychological cost to legal processes and bureaucracy.

Posted October 4, 2026

Key points
  • Navigating the legal system can lead to feelings of learned helplessness and ambiguous grief.
  • Stress and distress can be caused by dehumanizing language and hypervigilance.
  • Extended uncertainties can negatively affect mood, relationships, health, and overall well-being.

High-profile legal cases, from murder to deportation, capture public attention and often become the focus of public debate. But amidst the legal details and defenses are human beings who are significantly affected by the process.

Source: Wesley Tingey/Unsplash

We know there are multiple sides to every story and often the larger truth lies somewhere in between, but our perception is heavily influenced by the flashy headlines, first splashy photos, or initial public narrative that is offered. And with today’s news cycle being nonstop and instantaneous, there is a public exposure that adds extra layers of complexity.

Any legal proceeding is costly and stressful, but several specific factors add to the experience being especially difficult from a mental health perspective.

Trauma is a complex word that is overused in our modern world, but most anyone who has been involved in a lengthy court case with significant stakes could be found to be experiencing some aspects of trauma.

An important note about the concept of trauma is that it is more about what is experienced on the inside than about a specific triggering event or circumstances. Humans can experience the same situations yet have very different reactions; however, there are some situations, like intensive court involvement, that tend to be universally difficult.

Individual legal situations naturally vary, but three specific facets of courtroom involvement can add to the potential for experiencing trauma.

1. Just-World Hypothesis Is Shattered

Source: Victor Moragriega/Pexels

In psychology, there is a belief (or cognitive bias) that good things happen to good people and bad things happen to bad people. Most people try to do the right thing and are naturally shocked when their world is turned upside-down by an event. When a horrendous event occurs or someone feels falsely accused of something, this idea of things being fair and right is shattered. The way in which one’s world and one’s worldview can be changed in an instant can leave someone dazed and stunned.

Many of us believe that being kind, conscientious, and well-behaved will keep us generally safe; however, a momentous event can suddenly result in someone thinking they can’t protect or impact themselves or their families. Such an event may lead to someone suddenly being forced to manage a sense of injustice and spiral into a phase of learned helplessness (feeling like we have little power or agency to affect change). Shifting from a trusting to a distrusting stance is jarring and devastating. We humans often then construct narratives, infer motives, and seek out meaning; we may be trying to make sense of the situation but often the assumptions are misguided or mistaken.

This can feel like there is suddenly a gaping hole in our assumed safety net.

Dehumanizing Language Is Demeaning

The language of the courts is designed to be focused on specific statutes, dates, and specific details. The benefit of this precision is an attempt at exactness and an effort at upholding the laws that serve to protect us; however, the language can also feel impersonal, cold, and overly simplified. Legal systems wouldn’t work as well if they were based only on emotions or if counsel couldn’t distance themselves from some of the material, but the result is that the emotion-laden humans involved can feel misunderstood and reduced to details that are dehumanizing. Laws and rules are designed to protect us from arbitrary individual judgment, but that same objective language can also sterilize or minimize deeply emotional, life-shattering events.

Source: Sasun Bughdaryan/Unsplash

For most people who don’t work in the legal system, the information can also feel confusing, overwhelming, unyielding, and sometimes belittling. Being suddenly thrown into the world of courtroom communications can feel like being dropped into a foreign country where others are speaking a language that you barely comprehend. Understanding questions asked and how/if to answer them is often much more complex than imagined. This can lead to lowered confidence, increased trepidation, and overall distress.

The bureaucratic buffer of legalese does have a purpose but can feel like a muted, masked response during a pointedly stressful and vulnerable time.

Long-Term Uncertainty Is Destabilizing

Any serious legal proceedings often involve many months and sometimes years of preparing, waiting, and engaging in a legal labyrinth. The uncertainty and hypervigilance are difficult on the human nervous system, as humans are not designed to be in a sympathetic nervous system response (known as the fight-or-flight reaction) for extended periods of time. Anticipatory anxiety (awaiting an unknown in the future), anticipatory grief (awaiting a possible future loss), and ambiguous loss or grief (unclear or unending losses without a clear resolution) are common in various situations, including extensive legal battles, and these are further complications during extended periods of uncertainty.

Source: Fotografia Lui Vlad/Pexels

All of these factors can add to difficulties in mood, anxiety, relationships, work, self-confidence, and overall health. Attempting to go on with regular life while a decision hangs overhead is difficult at best and destabilizing at worst. Humans function better with knowing what to expect and with routines, but a significant and potentially life-changing unknown simply can’t be ignored or forgotten for very long. Individuals cannot comfortably plan, invest in their communities, or feel secure with such ambiguity in the future.

Like being stuck in a maze of an indeterminate size with exits unknown, the psychological toll of being in ongoing limbo can wreak havoc on the brain and body.

Maintain Perspective

No matter what the latest headline, public opinion, or social media narrative is swirling for a current court case, all of us can benefit from an increased understanding of the human factors involved in any complicated case. Perspective doesn’t shift the facts of the case nor the final rulings, but it can allow us to be a bit more sensitive to the human trauma involved without overfocusing on the drama.

item.title: Stone Age Brains and the Adapting Mind
item.description:
Evolutionary Psychology

Stone Age Brains and the Adapting Mind

Our Stone Age brains have evolved since the Neolithic began.

Posted October 4, 2026

Key points
  • Evolutionary psychology sits on a Stone Age foundation.
  • Recent evidence suggests strong directional selection on complex human traits.
  • Natural selection accelerated with the Neolithic Revolution.
The Thinker/Rodin
Source: Wikimedia Commons

“The evolved structure of the human mind is adapted to the way of life of Pleistocene hunter-gatherers.” —Leda Cosmides, John Tooby, and Jerome Barkow, 1992

“Evolution is happening constantly, and it’s rapidly responding to the cultural, economic, and environmental changes we’ve imposed on ourselves over the last 10,000 years.” —David Reich 2026

A generation ago, in the summer of 1992, the Canadian anthropologist Jerry Barkow and his Harvard-educated collaborators, John Tooby and Leda Cosmides, published their landmark volume, The Adapted Mind. It set evolutionary psychology on a Stone Age foundation. “Our ancestors spent the last two million years as Pleistocene hunter-gatherers, and, of course, several hundred million years before that as one kind of forager or another. Homo sapiens is adapted to Pleistocene conditions,” they wrote in their introduction. A year later, Cosmides and Tooby doubled down. “Our ancestors spent well over 99 percent of our species’ evolutionary history living in hunter-gatherer societies. That means our forebears lived in small, nomadic bands of a few dozen individuals who got all of their food each day by gathering plants and by hunting animals.” We might not be foragers anymore, but we’re all living with Stone Age brains.

Last April, a paper in Nature pushed back. Ali Akbari and his coauthors, many from David Reich’s lab at Harvard, analyzed ancient DNA samples from almost 16,000 West Eurasians, and found that hundreds of alleles have been affected by strong directional selection—over just the past 10,000 years. Genes involved in immunity were most likely to show evidence of selective pressure: viruses evolve fast, and hosts evolve defenses against them. But hundreds of changes have occurred in alleles that predict complex traits—from skin color to body fat, from mental illness to cognitive performance. “It’s like we had in our heads that a few hundred thousand years ago we had reached some kind of evolutionary optimization,” Reich remarked. And the pace has accelerated. The evidence suggests stronger selection over the past 5000 years than over the 5000 years before. As Akbari summed up: “Natural selection has not slowed down.”

We should not be surprised. Other genetic studies done over the past few decades have shown dramatically high rates of differential reproduction, or natural selection, since the Neolithic Revolution.

In a 2003 study, Tatiana Zerjal, working with a team under Chris Tyler-Smith at Oxford, found a Y-chromosome lineage in 8 percent of men across a vast swath of Asia, or roughly 1 in 200 men worldwide. They suggested that lineage might have originated in Mongolia around 1000 years ago; perhaps spread by the male-line descendants of Genghis Khan. More than one of Genghis’s sons and grandsons were among dynasty founders: Ögedei and Tolui succeeded their father; Changatai founded a khanate in Central Asia; Batu founded the Golden Horde; Kublai, a son of Tolui, founded the Yuan dynasty in China. Whether or not the cluster originated with those khans, Mongol genes spread around. As Zerjal and colleagues pointed out: “Such a rapid spread cannot have occurred by chance; it must have been a result of selection.”

Another 2015 study by Monika Karmin and coauthors, working with Toomas Kivisild at Cambridge, found a Y-chromosome bottleneck around the time the Neolithic began. In their sample, the breeding population of males was a fraction of the breeding population of females. There were 17 breeding women for every one breeding man. Male Ne, or effective breeding population, bottomed out at around 5000 BC in the Near East, and around 3000 BC in Europe. Those numbers track back to the rise of civilizations, and of reproductive variance. When asked to explain the result, Melissa Wilson, who was one of the contributors, did not mince words: “It wasn’t like there was a mass death of males. They were there, so what were they doing?”

History suggests that they might have been soldiers, or slaves, or celibates, or castrated civil servants; because after we settled down, inequality went up.

A few kilometers from the west bank of the Nile, in the Valley of the Kings near Thebes, the New Kingdom pharaoh Ramesses II cut a tomb out of the rock for his sons. More than 3 millennia later, in February 1995, American archaeologist Kent Weeks and his team crawled through a tight gap and broke into the vast labyrinth of interconnected corridors and rooms that make up the largest Egyptian tomb. Close to 150 of those chambers have been mapped by now, many with reliefs or alabaster canopic jars that bear the names of Ramesses II’s sons. Some were generals or hereditary counts; others were chiefs of secrets or scribes. Weeks guessed there were over 50. And there would have been roughly as many daughters. Shelley imagined the lone and level sands that stretched away from Ozymandias’ ruins. But his posterity probably lived on.

More than seven centuries before KV5 was rediscovered, in August 1275, Marco Polo showed up at the Xanadu court of Kublai Khan, and was overwhelmed. Set on the southern edge of the Mongolian plateau, overlooking the Shandian River, sat a magnificent marble palace with gilded halls, a massive park filled with grasslands and game, and 10,000 white horses for the khan’s entourage, surrounded by towers and walls. Ming armies sacked Xanadu, or Shangdu, in 1369. But excavations since 2012 have corroborated estimates from the Mongol dynastic history, or Yuan Shi, of a population of over 100,000. Some of those women were at the khan's disposal. Polo counted the 6 consorts sent to him every 3 nights: “And so, throughout the year, there are reliefs of maidens by 6 and 6.” The upshots were 22 sons by his 4 wives, with at least 25 sons by his concubines. As Coleridge would suppose:

His flashing eyes, his floating hair!
Weave a circle around him thrice,
And close your eyes with holy dread,
For he on honey-dew hath fed,
And drunk the milk of Paradise.

Several hundred million years ago, our ancestors were coming out of the oceans. A few million years ago, they were coming out of the trees. Bipedalism was evolving up to 2 million years ago; brain size accelerated at around the same time, from roughly 450 to 1300 ccs. Homo sapiens, with slower-developing children and more cooperative groups to care for them, is no older than about 300,000 years.

Our ancestors changed a lot over the last few thousand, and millions, of years. And we’re changing now.

item.title: Can a 'Food Divorce' Help or Hurt Your Relationship?
item.description:
Relationships

Can a 'Food Divorce' Help or Hurt Your Relationship?

Shopping, cooking, and eating can be central to a relationship.

Posted October 4, 2026

Key points
  • A "food divorce" is when you and your partner no longer shop for groceries, cook, or eat together regularly.
  • Food-related activities can be an important way for a couple to coordinate, communicate, and bond together.
  • Differing food preferences and needs, as well as scheduling and personality challenges, can interfere.
A "food divorce" is when you and your partner no longer shop for groceries, cook, or eat together, even though you may be living together.
Source: Milles Studio/Shutterstock

Here's some food for thought. Can a divorce actually save your relationship—a "food divorce," that is? A "food divorce" is term that's being used on the internet to describe a situation where you and your partner no longer shop for groceries, cook, or eat together, even though you may be living together. Instead, each of you does the meal thing independently or even separately. You are essentially separated like oil and vinegar when it comes to things food.

Food Can Be Quite Central to a Relationship

Now, this might be quite different from what you first envisioned when you began cohabiting with your partner. After all, sharing food duties and activities is what many couples do. It certainly can be a time saver and nice having someone else available to take up the shopping and cooking slack whenever you are feeling tired. It can be a cost-saver, too, as you can finally buy and use completely that 6-pound tub of guacamole or 72-pound parmigiano reggiano cheese wheel found at Costco.

Beyond that, food can facilitate key conversations and bonding. What better time to talk about your day and feelings than a bucket of bubble and squeak or whatever the two of you can enjoy preparing and eating together. Moreover, cooking for and feeding each other are often ways to show mutual caring and appreciation.

Yes, food can be quite central to a relationship. After all, eating is one thing that all humans must do each day along with sleeping and going to the bathroom. And the last thing may not be something you want to share while the second-to-last thing may not offer the best way to talk.

However, There Can Be Disagreements Over Food

On the flip side, meals can serve up some real disagreements—especially when you have very different shopping, cooking, and eating preferences. What if, for example, your partner wants all meals to be low carb when you think bread is the best thing since, well, sliced bread? Differences in food preferences can get very serious when allergies or other medical issues are involved.

Even if you do like the same food, cooking and eating can have a way of bringing out the Gordon Ramsay in some—making them picky, demanding, and critical and plunging the meal experience into a Hell's Kitchen of sorts. Additionally, coordinating the logistics like the timing, scheduling, and location of meals can be challenging. Divergent work demands and lifestyle preferences can make it more difficult to eat together like when your partner is at sea on an aircraft carrier and you don't want to swim that far.

Basically, food can be like fruitcake for a couple. When things are well-coordinated, it can lead to some fruitful connection. When the two of you are not on the same recipe page, it can drive you nuts. All of this, when unaddressed, can end up eating away at your connection, lead to resentment, and end up spilling over to the rest of your relationship.

Address Any Food Disagreements As Soon As Possible

Therefore, it's not a good idea to let food-related disagreements slide like pudding on an ice sculpture. Instead, put them front and center as soon as possible in a discussion with your partner. And don't be mealy-mouthed and sugar-coat things. Be frank and open-faced about what's bothering you.

Ideally, the two of you can make some concessions and compromises. Maybe you and your partner can find better ways to work together and coordinate. That could actually get the rest of your relationship cooking in a good way. Plus, you could even help each other to eat more healthily and be less picky about things.

A Food Divorce Is a Possible Option

Source: cottonbro studio/Pexels

However, if you do find food-related coordinating and compromising too difficult, then yes, a "food divorce" could be something to consider. A couple doesn't have to do everything together in a joined-at-the-hip manner. In fact, it can be natural and even healthier to do some things separately, especially things where you have divergent preferences and viewpoints.

Now, a "food divorce" can range greatly in its implementation. One end of the spectrum is still eating together but often eating completely different things while maintaining joint custody over some things like special desserts. The other end of the spectrum is when the two of you do all food things completely independently and separately. So, a very mild food divorce may not even be a big deal.

A "food divorce" could be an effective solution if the rest of your relationship is peachy keen—just not peach melba keen—and the only thing salty about your pairing is food-related. As long as your relationship already has plenty of other ways to bond and communicate and remain a great pair, then it may be fine that you are not having pears together.

A Food Divorce Can Lead to Further Deterioration of the Relationship

The risk, though, is that a "food divorce," especially a more drastic one, ends up being just an appetizer for an eventual full divorce. When you start doing one big set of activities separately, what's to prevent the two of you from eventually doing other things separately? Without set ways and times to keep coordinating and communicating as a couple, the two of you can become more and more like roommates rather than romantic partners.

Moreover, food-related disagreements could just be other underlying issues bubbling to the surface. They could represent an unwillingness to compromise, an inability to communicate and coordinate, or a lack of caring in general—you know, stuff that could end up wrecking a relationship. In other words, could insisting on eating shellfish while the other has shellfish allergies be ultimately a selfish act? If food incompatibility is a sign of other deeper incompatibilities, then you've got bigger fish to fry.

So before jumping right to a "food divorce," you may want to explore and sample other options first and better understand what the true issues are. At least, check whether the other aspects of your relationship are solid before going through any divorce proceedings. You may even want to "turnip" the communicating, coordinating, and bonding in other ways in order to compensate. Just make sure any desire or plan for a food divorce is not divorced from the reality of the rest of your relationship.
